confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gibson, Lorna F. 1956. Pame (Otomi) phonemics and morphophonemics. International Journal of American Linguistics 22(4): 242-265. DOI 10.1086/464377. Rosetta Project 7-page excerpt (pp. 242-248), archive.org.
catalog_locator: §2.6 Tone-stress, pp. 258-259 of IJAL 22(4); §1.1 Word and §1.2 Syllable, pp. 243-244; p. 244 cross-reference to secondary stress, rule stated on p. 259
catalog_quote: 2.6. Significant tone falls on the same syllables as unpredictable, primary stress, forming three phonemes of tone-stress: high, marked /´/, low, marked /`/, and falling glide, marked /ˆ/. Tone-stress is marked over the first vowel of any vowel cluster, since that is where onset of stress begins. All other syllables have predictable tone and predictable secondary stress or lack of stress, and are left unmarked. [p. 243, §1.1] A word in Pame may be defined phonologically as a minimal utterance. A simple word has one and only one phoneme of tone-stress. Compound words may have two phonemes of tone-stress. ... Clitics are without tone-stress, except for the alternate mmba of the postclitic mba it is probable. [§1.2] Included are syllables of pattern -CV(VCCCC) ... which, as a matter of fact, never carry contrastive tone-stress because they constitute the second syllable of a stem having tone-stress on the first syllable or on the prefix, e.g. wómma?aigŋky they are standing.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each simple word has exactly one primary stress, whose position is not predictable from phonological shape; the stressed syllable is also the only one that carries contrastive tone (high, low, falling — Gibson 1956; falling reanalysed as H+L across a vowel cluster in Gibson, Olson & Olson 1963). The position is constrained morphologically: stress falls either on the (usually final, monosyllabic) root or on a prefix syllable — Gibson 1956 §1.2 says a stem's second syllable never carries contrastive tone-stress, stress being on the stem's first syllable or on the prefix; Herce 2024 §2 states that when stress is on the final syllable it coincides with the stem, and when on the penult/antepenult it is on the prefix (then only high tone). Herce 2025 (p. 415) confirms 'any syllable can be stressed'; in verbs the prefix-vs-root placement is a lexical/inflectional class property, alternating within some paradigms (§3.3).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Gibson 1956 p. 248: unstressed syllables have 'predictable secondary stress or lack of stress' (unmarked); p. 244 mentions 'the secondary stressed syllable of a two-syllable word (i.e., second syllable preceded by CVCC-, as described in 2.6.)' — the full rule is on p. 249, not in the excerpt.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics carry no tone-stress except the utterance-initial alternant mmba (p. 243); compounds may carry two tone-stresses (three compounds listed, p. 243); tone-stress on a syllabic nasal only in m.mba (p. 244); the second vowel of a V-glottal-V sequence is never stressed (Herce 2025 fn. 1, p. 414).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, defined as a minimal utterance (Gibson 1956 §1.1); proclitics/postclitics are stressless and attach to the adjacent word; word boundaries in utterances are identified partly by tone-stress. Statements are about lexical/citation forms and paradigm forms, not phrasal prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Gibson 1956 (fn. 1, p. 242) calls her variety 'that dialect of North Pame spoken in and around the monolingual center of Santa María Acapulco'; in current classification (Glottolog/ISO) Santa María Acapulco Pame is Central Pame [pbs] cent2145 — Herce 2024/2025 use 'Central Pame' for the same variety and cite Gibson 1956 as its phonology. 'Northern Pame' in modern usage (Avelino 1997/2004, Berthiaume 2003; La Palma, Alaquines, Ciudad del Maíz) is [pmq] nort2984, so Glottolog's placement of Avelino 1997 'Pame Norte' under cent2145 looks misfiled. The Schuller 1925 edition of Fray Francisco Valle's 18th-century grammar concerns the Sierra Gorda Pame (Jalpan, Landa, Tilaco), i.e. the Southern Pame area (sout2999), not Central Pame.

new_statements.quote: [fn. 1, PDF p. 46] The analysis presented here is based on the speech of Cresenciano Mar, twenty eight years old, a member of a speech community numbering about 1300 Indians in the area of Santa Maria Acapulco, S.L.P. ... There are three phonemes of tone-stress, high ( ´ ), low ( ` ), and falling ( ^ ); only one tone-stress may occur with each word and it is written over the vowel which takes the onset of the tone-stress, although all vowels in clusters do share the particular tone-stress present. [sec. 6.1, typescript p. 13, PDF p. 14] If a stem occurs with a prefix having tone-stress, the stem tone-stress is lost and that of the prefix is retained.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the existing Gibson 1956 statement (three tone-stress phonemes on an unpredictable primary-stressed syllable, marked at onset of a vowel cluster). Olson adds that only one tone-stress occurs per word and that a tone-stress-bearing prefix displaces the stem's tone-stress, i.e. placement is morphologically conditioned rather than fixed; this is compatible with (and anticipates) Herce 2024/2025's description of stress on the stem (final) or on a prefix (penult/antepenult). The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so nothing is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pame (Santa Maria Acapulco) has three combined 'tone-stress' phonemes (high, low, falling); exactly one tone-stress occurs per word (culminative), marked on the vowel where its onset begins. Its position is not given by a phonological rule: stems carry their own tone-stress, and certain verb prefixes carry inherent tone-stress; when such a prefix is attached, the stem loses its tone-stress and the prefix's is kept, so placement (stem-final vs. prefix syllable) is determined lexically/morphologically by which morphemes are present. Vowels in 'unstressed' second syllables of stems are subject to loss (sec. 6.5.1), confirming an unstressed/stressed contrast within stems.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; only one tone-stress per word is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixes with inherent tone-stress override the stem's tone-stress (sec. 6.1); fn. 4 notes a prefix allomorph with 'discontinuous tone' replacing the stem tone-stress; fn. 11: 'Falling tone-stress replaces high tone-stress' in a particular allomorph context. No phonological placement rule is given; the note defers to Gibson's then-unpublished 'Pame (Otomi) Phonemics and Morphophonemics' for the phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Olson's footnote 1 identifies the data as the speech of one 28-year-old speaker from the Santa Maria Acapulco, S.L.P. community (data gathered 1951-2), i.e. exactly the catalog's 'Pame, Santa Maria Acapulco dialect' (Central Pame, pbs). The footnote's typed cross-reference calls Gibson's phonology 'of North Pame', hand-corrected on the typescript to 'Pame (Otomi) Phonemics and Morphophonemics' (= Gibson 1956, IJAL); this is the older SIL label for the same Santa Maria Acapulco variety, not Glottolog's Northern Pame (pmq).

tone_statements.quote: Central Pame is an Otomanguean language whose word prosodic system has been impressionistically described as one with stress and tone, with a three-way tonal contrast. ... Results indicate that duration is longer in stressed than in deaccented syllables. Intensity and, to some degree, spectral tilt measures are also affected by stress. Additionally, we find evidence for a three-way tonal contrast marked with fundamental frequency and duration and which varies between female and male speakers.
tone_statements.summary: Word stress + 3-way tonal contrast (H, L, falling per Gibson) on the stressed syllable, acoustically confirmed (F0 + duration).

sources.note: Orthographic note pp. 125-126 only: revises the 1956 tone-stress analysis (falling tone-stress reinterpreted as high on the first vowel of a cluster followed by low on the rest; rising tone-stress added); high tone-stress may fall on a single vowel; low tone-stress marked where the onset of stress begins. No positional rule for stress.

sources.quote: Central Pame is an Otomanguean language whose word prosodic system has been impressionistically described as one with stress and tone, with a three-way tonal contrast. ... Results indicate that duration is longer in stressed than in deaccented syllables. Intensity and, to some degree, spectral tilt measures are also affected by stress. Additionally, we find evidence for a three-way tonal contrast marked with fundamental frequency and duration and which varies between female and male speakers.
sources.note: First quantitative acoustic study of Central Pame word prosody; tests the impressionistic description (stress plus a three-way tonal contrast on the stressed syllable); finds duration (and intensity, spectral tilt) cue stress, and confirms a three-way tonal contrast carried by F0 and duration, realised differently by female and male speakers.
